title: If the Romans prayed with one accord
source_text: Εἶτα ἑαυτοῦ μὴ ἀκούσας ὁ Κέλσος, τὰ ἀνακόλουθα εἰπόντος τῷ εἰ γὰρ τὸ αὐτό σοι ποιήσειαν ἅπαντες, φησίν· οὐ μὲν δὴ τοῦτο φήσεις. ὡς, ἂν πεισθέντες σοι Ῥωμαῖοι καὶ τῶν νενομισμένων αὐτοῖς πρὸς θεούς τε καὶ ἀνθρώπους ἀμελήσαντες τὸν σὸν Ὕψιστον, ἢ ὅντινα βούλει, προσκαλέσωνται. καταβὰς ὑπερμαχεῖται αὐτῶν, καὶ οὐδεμιᾶς ἄλλης ἀλκῆς δεήσει. καὶ γὰρ πρότερον ὁ αὐτὸς θεὸς τοῖς προσέχουσιν αὐτῷ ταῦτά τε καὶ πολὺ μείζω τούτων, ὡς ὑμεῖς φατε, ὑπισχνούμενος ὁρᾶτε ὅσα ὠφέλησεν ἐκείνους τε καὶ ὑμᾶς· ὧν τοῖς μὲν ἀντὶ (τοῦ) γῆς ἁπάσης εἶναι δεσπόταις οὐδ᾿ ὁποία τις βῶλος οὐδ᾿ ἑστία λείπεται, ὑμῶν δὲ κἂν πλανᾶταί τις ἔτι λανθάνων, ἀλλὰ ζητεῖται πρὸς θανάτου δίκην. ἐπεὶ δὲ καθ᾿ ὑπόθεσιν ζητεῖ, εἰ πεισθέντες Ῥωμαῖοι τῷ Χριστιανῶν λόγῳ, τῶν πρὸς τοὺς νενομισμένους θεοὺς ἀμελήσαντες καὶ τῶν κατὰ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους προτέρων νόμων, τὸν Υψιστον σέβοιντο, τί ἂν ἀπαντήσαι· ἄκουε τί ἀρέσκει περὶ τούτων ἡμῖν. φαμὲν ὅτι, εἴπερ, „ἂν δύο συμφωνῶσιν“ ἐξ ἡμῶν „ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς περὶ παντὸς πράγματος, οὗ ἐὰν αἰτήσωνται γενήσεται αὐτοῖς παρὰ τοῦ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς πατρὸς“ τῶν δικαίων· χαίρει γὰρ συμφωνίᾳ τῶν λογικῶν ζῴων ὁ θεὸς καὶ ἐκτρέπεται τὴν διαφωνίαν· τί χρὴ νομίζειν, εἰ μὴ μόνον ὡς νῦν πάνυ ὀλίγοι συμφωνοῖεν ἀλλὰ πᾶσα ἡ ὑπὸ Ῥωμαίων ἀρχή; εὔξονται γὰρ τῷ καὶ πρότερον εἰπόντι πρὸς τοὺς Ἑβραίους καταδιωκομένους ὑπὸ Αἰγυπτίων λόγῳ· „κύριος πολεμήσει ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν, καὶ ὑμεῖς σιγήσεσθε,“ καὶ μετὰ πάσης συμφωνίας εὐξάμενοι πολλῷ πλείονας δυνήσονται καταλῦσαι ἐχθροὺς ἐπιδιώκοντας, ἢ οὓς καθεῖλεν ἡ Μωϋσέως πρὸς τὸν θεὸν βοῶντος καὶ τῶν σὺν αὐτῷ εὐχή. ἃ δ᾿ ὑπέσχετο ὁ θεὸς τοῖς τηροῦσι τὸν νόμον εἰ μὴ γεγένηται, οὐ τῷ ψεύδεσθαι τὸν θεὸν οὐ γεγένηται ἀλλὰ τῷ ἐπὶ συνθήκαις γεγονέναι τὰς ἐπαγγελίας, ταῖς περὶ τοῦ τηρεῖν τὸν νόμον καὶ τὸν κατὰ τὸν νόμον βίον. καὶ εἰ οὔτε βῶλος οὔθ᾿ ἑστία Ἰουδαίοις καταλείπεται τοῖς τὰς ἐπαγγελίας ἐπὶ συνθήκαις εἰληφόσιν, αἰτιατέον πᾶσαν μὲν αὐτῶν τὴν παρανομίαν ἐξαιρέτως δὲ τὴν κατὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ.
pass_a_gloss: Then Celsus, not having listened to himself, having said the inconsequent things (ἀνακόλουθα) in 'for if all were to do the same as you', says: 'You will surely not say this: that if the Romans, persuaded by you and having neglected (ἀμελέω) their customary (νενομισμένα) things toward gods and men, call upon (προσκαλέομαι) your Most High (Ὕψιστος), or whomever you wish, having come down (καταβαίνω) he will fight for (ὑπερμαχέω) them, and there will be need of no other strength/help (ἀλκή). For formerly too the same God, promising (ὑπισχνέομαι) these things and much greater than these to those giving heed (προσέχω) to him, as you say, you see how much he has benefited (ὠφελέω) both them and you; of whom, to the former, instead of being masters (δεσπότης) of all the earth, not even any clod (βῶλος) or hearth (ἑστία) is left, and of you, even if someone still wanders (πλανάομαι) escaping notice (λανθάνω), yet he is sought (ζητέω) for the penalty (δίκη) of death.' But since he inquires by hypothesis (καθ᾿ ὑπόθεσιν), if the Romans, persuaded by the doctrine (λόγος) of the Christians, having neglected the things toward the customary gods and the former laws among men, were to revere the Most High, what would happen (ἀπαντάω); hear what pleases us about these things. We say that, if indeed 'if two agree (συμφωνέω)' of us 'on the earth about every matter (πρᾶγμα), whatever they ask (αἰτέω) will come to be for them from the Father in the heavens' of the righteous (for God rejoices in concord (συμφωνία) of rational living beings (λογικὰ ζῷα) and turns away (ἐκτρέπομαι) from discord (διαφωνία)), what must one think, if not only, as now, very few were to agree, but all the empire (ἀρχή) under the Romans? For they will pray to the one who also formerly spoke to the Hebrews being pursued (καταδιώκω) by the Egyptians, the Word (λόγος): 'The Lord will fight (πολεμέω) for you, and you will be silent (σιγάω)'; and having prayed with all concord they will be able to destroy (καταλύω) many more pursuing (ἐπιδιώκω) enemies than those whom the prayer (εὐχή) of Moses crying out (βοάω) to God and of those with him brought down (καθαιρέω). But the things which God promised to those keeping (τηρέω) the law, if they have not come about, not by God's lying (ψεύδομαι) have they not come about, but by the promises (ἐπαγγελία) having been made on covenants/conditions (συνθῆκαι), those about keeping the law and the life according to the law. And if neither clod nor hearth is left to the Jews, who received the promises on conditions, one must blame (αἰτιατέον) all their lawlessness (παρανομία), but especially (ἐξαιρέτως) that against Jesus.
pass_b_english: Then Celsus, not hearing himself as he says things that do not hang together in the words, “For if all were to do the same as you,” says: “Surely you will not say this: that if the Romans, persuaded by you, were to neglect their customary duties toward gods and men and call upon your Most High, or whoever you like, he will come down and fight for them, and they will need no other help. For before this too the same God, as you say, promised these things and far greater ones to those who gave heed to him; and you see how much he has helped both them and you. Of them, instead of their being masters of the whole earth, not so much as a clod of soil or a hearth is left; and of you, if any still wanders about in hiding, yet he is hunted down to be punished with death.”

But since he asks, by way of supposition, what would happen if the Romans, persuaded by the doctrine of the Christians, were to neglect their duties toward the customary gods and the former laws among men and worship the Most High, hear what we hold about this. We say that if “two” of us “agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them by the Father” of the righteous, “who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:19) — for God rejoices in the concord of rational beings and turns away from discord — what must we think if not only a very few, as now, were to agree, but the whole empire under the Romans? For they will pray to the Word who said long ago to the Hebrews when the Egyptians were pursuing them: “The Lord will fight for you, and you shall keep silent” (Exodus 14:14). And praying in complete concord they will be able to destroy far more enemies who pursue them than those whom the prayer of Moses and of those with him brought down, when he cried out to God (compare Exodus 14:15).

If the things that God promised to those who keep the law have not come about, they have failed to come about not because God lies, but because the promises were made on conditions, the conditions of keeping the law and living according to the law. And if neither clod nor hearth is left to the Jews, who received the promises on conditions, the blame must be laid on all their transgression of the law, and above all on their transgression against Jesus.

choices.choice: Koetschau’s punctuation breaks Celsus’s sentence with full stops at ‘προσκαλέσωνται’ and ‘ὑπερμαχεῖται’; read as one continuous hypothetical. In Celsus’s words ‘them’ (ἐκείνους, τοῖς μέν) are the Jews, as Origen’s reply makes explicit; not supplied in Celsus’s text. The supplement (τοῦ) before γῆς is the editor’s. ‘what would happen’ renders τί ἂν ἀπαντήσαι (literally ‘what would turn out/result’); could also be taken ‘what we would answer’. Matthew 18:19 is quoted with Origen’s changes: ἐξ ἡμῶν (‘of us’) for ἐξ ὑμῶν, and ‘the Father of the righteous who is in heaven’ for ‘my Father in heaven’; the words ‘of the righteous’ are kept outside the quotation marks as Origen’s own. ‘the Word who said’ renders τῷ ... εἰπόντι ... λόγῳ: Origen identifies the speaker of Exodus 14:14 with the Word. ‘when he cried out to God’ alludes to Exodus 14:15 (‘Why do you cry to me?’); βοῶντος is singular and goes with Moses, while the prayer (εὐχή) is that of Moses and of those with him. ‘they have failed to come about not because God lies’ keeps Origen’s repeated negative structure (οὐ τῷ ψεύδεσθαι ... οὐ γεγένηται). ‘not hearing himself as he says’ renders ἑαυτοῦ μὴ ἀκούσας ... εἰπόντος (genitive participle agreeing with ἑαυτοῦ).

'not listening to himself, though he has just said something that does not fit' -> 'not hearing himself as he says things that do not hang together' (εἰπόντος agrees with ἑαυτοῦ; 'though' was an added concession)
parenthesis on God's delight in concord set off with dashes so the long conditional reads clearly
'the prayer of Moses ... together with the prayer of those who were with him' -> 'the prayer of Moses and of those with him' (one εὐχή in the Greek)
Matthew 18:19, Exodus 14:14, Exodus 14:15 checked: correct; Celsus / Origen speakers checked

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; the English is from the Greek.
